<<민법  제169조(시효중단의 효력)>> 시효의 중단은 당사자 및 그 승계인간에만 효력이 있다.

<<민법  제170조(재판상의 청구와 시효중단)>> ①재판상의 청구는 소송의 각하, 기각 또는 취하의 경우에는 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

②전항의 경우에 6월내에 재판상의 청구, 파산절차참가, 압류 또는 가압류, 가처분을 한 때에는 시효는 최초의 재판상 청구로 인하여 중단된 것으로 본다.

<<민법  제171조(파산절차참가와 시효중단)>> 파산절차참가는 채권자가 이를 취소하거나 그 청구가 각하된 때에는 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

<<민법  제172조(지급명령과 시효중단)>> 지급명령은 채권자가 법정기간내에 가집행신청을 하지 아니함으로 인하여 그 효력을 잃은 때에는 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

<<민법  제173조(화해를 위한 소환, 임의출석과 시효중단)>> 화해를 위한 소환은 상대방이 출석하지 아니 하거나 화해가 성립되지 아니한 때에는 1월내에 소를 제기하지 아니하면 시효중단의 효력이 없다. 임의출석의 경우에 화해가 성립되지 아니한 때에도 그러하다.

<<민법  제174조(최고와 시효중단)>> 최고는 6월내에 재판상의 청구, 파산절차참가, 화해를 위한 소환, 임의출석, 압류 또는 가압류, 가처분을 하지 아니하면 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

<<민법  제175조(압류, 가압류, 가처분과 시효중단)>> 압류, 가압류 및 가처분은 권리자의 청구에 의하여 또는 법률의 규정에 따르지 아니함으로 인하여 취소된 때에는 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

<<민법  제176조(압류, 가압류, 가처분과 시효중단)>> 압류, 가압류 및 가처분은 시효의 이익을 받은 자에 대하여 하지 아니한 때에는 이를 그에게 통지한 후가 아니면 시효중단의 효력이 없다.

<<민법  제177조(승인과 시효중단)>> 시효중단의 효력있는 승인에는 상대방의 권리에 관한 처분의 능력이나 권한있음을 요하지 아니한다.

<<민법  제178조(중단후에 시효진행)>> ①시효가 중단된 때에는 중단까지에 경과한 시효기간은 이를 산입하지 아니하고 중단사유가 종료한 때로부터 새로이 진행한다.

②재판상의 청구로 인하여 중단한 시효는 전항의 규정에 의하여 재판이 확정된 때로부터 새로이 진행한다.

<<민법  제179조(제한능력자의 시효정지)>> 소멸시효의 기간만료 전 6개월 내에 제한능력자에게 법정대리인이 없는 경우에는 그가 능력자가 되거나 법정대리인이 취임한 때부터 6개월 내에는 시효가 완성되지 아니한다.

[전문개정 2011. 3. 7.]

<<민법  제180조(재산관리자에 대한 제한능력자의 권리, 부부 사이의 권리와 시효정지)>> ① 재산을 관리하는 아버지, 어머니 또는 후견인에 대한 제한능력자의 권리는 그가 능력자가 되거나 후임 법정대리인이 취임한 때부터 6개월 내에는 소멸시효가 완성되지 아니한다.

② 부부 중 한쪽이 다른 쪽에 대하여 가지는 권리는 혼인관계가 종료된 때부터 6개월 내에는 소멸시효가 완성되지 아니한다.

[전문개정 2011. 3. 7.]

<<민법  제181조(상속재산에 관한 권리와 시효정지)>> 상속재산에 속한 권리나 상속재산에 대한 권리는 상속인의 확정, 관리인의 선임 또는 파산선고가 있는 때로부터 6월내에는 소멸시효가 완성하지 아니한다.

<<민법  제182조(천재 기타 사변과 시효정지)>> 천재 기타 사변으로 인하여 소멸시효를 중단할 수 없을 때에는 그 사유가 종료한 때로부터 1월내에는 시효가 완성하지 아니한다.

<<민법 제184조(시효의 이익의 포기 기타)>> ①소멸시효의 이익은 미리 포기하지 못한다.

②소멸시효는 법률행위에 의하여 이를 배제, 연장 또는 가중할 수 없으나 이를 단축 또는 경감할 수 있다.

<<지방재정법 제82조(금전채권과 채무의 소멸시효)>> ① 금전의 지급을 목적으로 하는 지방자치단체의 권리는 시효에 관하여 다른 법률에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우를 제외하고는 5년간 행사하지 아니하면 소멸시효가 완성한다.

② 금전의 지급을 목적으로 하는 지방자치단체에 대한 권리도 제1항과 같다.

[전문개정 2011. 8. 4.]

<<지방재정법 제83조(소멸시효의 중단과 정지)>> ① 금전의 지급을 목적으로 하는 지방자치단체의 권리에 관하여는 다른 법률에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우를 제외하고는 「민법」 중 소멸시효의 중단과 정지에 관한 규정을 준용한다.

② 금전의 지급을 목적으로 하는 지방자치단체에 대한 권리도 제1항과 같다.

[전문개정 2011. 8. 4.]

<<국가재정법 제96조(금전채권ㆍ채무의 소멸시효)>> ①금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리로서 시효에 관하여 다른 법률에 규정이 없는 것은 5년 동안 행사하지 아니하면 시효로 인하여 소멸한다.

②국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 제1항과 같다.

③금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리의 경우 소멸시효의 중단ㆍ정지 그 밖의 사항에 관하여 다른 법률의 규정이 없는 때에는 「민법」의 규정을 적용한다. 국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 같다. <개정 2020. 6. 9.>

④법령의 규정에 따라 국가가 행하는 납입의 고지는 시효중단의 효력이 있다.

<<헌법 제101조>> ①사법권은 법관으로 구성된 법원에 속한다.

②법원은 최고법원인 대법원과 각급법원으로 조직된다.

③법관의 자격은 법률로 정한다.

<<법제업무운영규정 제26조(법령해석의 요청)>> ① 중앙행정기관의 장은 지방자치단체의 장 또는 민원인으로부터 법률적 판단이 필요한 질의를 받는 등 법령을 운영ㆍ집행하는 과정에서 해석상 의문이 있는 경우에는 행정운영의 적법성과 타당성을 보장하기 위하여 「행정기본법」 제40조제3항에 따른 법령해석업무를 전문으로 하는 기관(민사ㆍ상사ㆍ형사, 행정소송, 국가배상 관계 법령 및 법무부 소관 법령과 다른 법령의 벌칙조항에 대한 해석인 경우에는 법무부를 말하고, 그 밖의 모든 행정 관계 법령의 해석인 경우에는 법제처를 말한다. 이하 “법령해석기관”이라 한다)에 법령해석을 요청하여야 한다. <개정 2021. 12. 1.>

② 중앙행정기관의 장은 다른 중앙행정기관 소관 법령에 대하여 제1항에 따른 해석 요청을 하려는 경우에는 해당 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장의 의견을 먼저 들어야 한다.

③ 지방자치단체의 장은 법령해석기관에 법령해석을 요청하려면 그 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장에게 법령해석을 요청하여 그 회신을 받아야 한다.

④ 지방자치단체의 장은 제3항의 회신 내용이 불명확(회신은 있으나 사실상 의견이 없는 경우를 포함한다)하거나 회신 내용에 이의가 있는 경우에는 그 회신 내용을 첨부하여 법령해석기관에 법령해석을 요청할 수 있다. 다만, 중앙행정기관의 장이 제3항에 따라 법령해석을 요청받고도 1개월 이내(특별한 사유가 있는 경우에는 그 지연 사유를 통보함으로써 1개월 이내의 기간을 정하여 한 차례만 연장할 수 있다)에 회신을 하지 아니하는 경우에는 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장의 회신 내용을 첨부하지 아니할 수 있다. <개정 2023. 6. 27.>

⑤ 제4항 본문에 따라 사실상 의견이 없는 중앙행정기관의 장의 회신 내용을 첨부한 법령해석 요청을 받거나 같은 항 단서에 따라 중앙행정기관의 장의 회신 내용을 첨부하지 않은 법령해석 요청을 받은 법령해석기관은 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장에게 해당 법령에 대한 의견을 요청하여야 하고, 그 요청을 받은 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장은 요청을 받은 날부터 10일 이내(특별한 사유가 있는 경우에는 그 지연 사유를 통보함으로써 10일 이내의 기간을 정하여 한 차례만 연장할 수 있다)에 법령해석기관으로 요청에 따른 회신을 하여야 한다.

⑥ 중앙행정기관의 장 또는 지방자치단체의 장은 제2항 또는 제4항에 따라 법령해석을 요청한 경우에는 그 사실을 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장에게 통보하여야 한다.

⑦ 민원인은 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장의 법령해석에 이의가 있는 경우에는 총리령으로 정하는 바에 따라 해당 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장에게 법령해석기관에 법령해석을 요청하도록 의뢰하거나 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장의 법령해석 의견을 덧붙여 직접 법령해석기관에 법령해석을 요청할 수 있다. 다만, 법무부장관이 민사ㆍ상사ㆍ형사, 행정소송, 국가배상 관계 법령 및 법무부 소관 법령에 대하여 법령해석을 한 경우는 제외한다. <개정 2021. 12. 1., 2023. 6. 27.>

⑧ 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장은 제7항에 따라 민원인으로부터 법령해석의 요청을 의뢰받으면 민원인에게 회신한 내용(민원인의 법령 질의사항을 포함한다)에 추가할 의견이 있는 경우 그 의견을 첨부하여 지체 없이 법령해석기관에 법령해석을 요청하여야 한다. 다만, 법령해석의 요청을 의뢰받은 사안이 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당되는 경우에는 법령해석을 요청하지 않을 수 있으며, 해당 민원인에게 그 사유를 명시하여 통지하여야 한다. <개정 2019. 8. 13., 2021. 12. 1.>

1. 제7항에 따른 법령해석 요청 기준에 맞지 않는 경우

2. 정립된 판례나 법령해석기관의 법령해석이 있는 경우

3. 구체적 사실인정에 관한 사항인 경우

4. 행정심판 또는 소송이 계속 중이거나 그 절차가 끝난 경우

5. 이미 행해진 구체적인 처분이나 행위의 위법ㆍ부당 여부에 관한 사항인 경우

6. 법령이 헌법 또는 상위 법령에 위반되는지에 관한 사항인 경우

7. 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 정책과 관련된 사항으로서 정책적 판단이나 중앙행정기관 사이의 협의를 통해 결정할 필요가 있는 경우

8. 해석 대상 법령이 특정되지 않는 경우

9. 법령해석을 요청하게 된 근거나 사유와 법령해석을 요청한 법령의 규정 사이에 연관성이 없는 등 법령해석 요청의 전제가 잘못되어 법령해석의 필요성이 인정되지 않는 경우

10. 법령의 규정상 명백하여 해석이 불필요한 경우

11. 그 밖에 제1호부터 제10호까지의 규정과 유사한 사유로서 명백히 법령해석이 필요하지 않다고 인정되는 경우

⑨ 법령해석기관은 제7항에 따라 민원인으로부터 직접 법령해석 요청을 받았을 때에는 즉시 그 사실을 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장에게 통보하여야 한다. <개정 2021. 12. 1.>

⑩ 제1항, 제4항, 제7항 및 제8항에 따라 법령해석을 요청받은 법령해석기관은 필요하다고 인정되는 경우 법령해석을 요청한 중앙행정기관의 장, 지방자치단체의 장 및 민원인에게 보완을 요청할 수 있다. <개정 2019. 8. 13., 2021. 12. 1.>

⑪ 법령해석기관은 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 경우에는 법령해석 요청을 반려한다. <신설 2019. 8. 13., 2021. 12. 1.>

1. 법령해석 요청이 제1항부터 제4항까지 및 제7항에 따른 법령해석 요청 기준에 맞지 않는 경우

2. 법령해석 요청이 제8항제2호부터 제11호까지의 규정에 해당하는 경우

3. 제10항에 따른 보완 요청에 응하지 않는 경우

② 중앙행정기관의 장은 다른 중앙행정기관 소관 법령에 대하여 제1항에 따른 해석 요청을 하려는 경우에는 해당 법령 소관 중앙행정기관의 장의 의견을 먼저 들어야 한다.

<<군인사법 제7조(의무복무기간)>> ① 장교, 준사관 및 부사관(지원에 의하지 아니하고 임용된 하사는 제외한다)의 의무복무기간은 다음 각 호와 같다. 다만, 전시ㆍ사변 등의 국가비상시에는 예외로 한다. <개정 2012. 12. 18., 2014. 3. 11., 2020. 12. 22.>

1. 장기복무 장교의 의무복무기간은 10년으로 한다. 다만, 장기복무 장교로 임용된 날부터 5년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역(轉役)을 지원할 수 있다.

2. 제1호에도 불구하고 해군의 장교 또는 공군의 장교로서 비행훈련과정을 수료하여 비행자격을 취득한 사람[회전익(回轉翼)항공기로 기종이 분류된 사람은 제외한다] 중 해군사관학교 또는 공군사관학교를 졸업한 사람의 의무복무기간은 15년, 그 외의 사람의 의무복무기간은 13년으로 한다. 다만, 장교로 임용된 날부터 5년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

3. 국방부장관은 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우에는 2년의 범위에서 제2호에 따른 의무복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

4. 단기복무 장교의 의무복무기간은 3년으로 한다. 다만, 육군3사관학교나 국군간호사관학교를 졸업한 사람은 6년으로 하고, 「병역법」 제57조제2항에 따른 학생군사교육단 사관후보생과정 출신 장교, 여군(女軍) 중 간호과 장교(국군간호사관학교를 졸업한 간호과 장교는 제외한다) 및 예비역 장교로서 전역 당시의 계급에 재임용된 중위 이상의 장교에 대하여는 국방부장관이 각 군의 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우 1년의 범위에서 그 복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

5. 준사관의 의무복무기간은 5년으로 한다. 다만, 대통령령으로 정하는 군의 필수 기술 분야에 종사하는 준사관(상사와 원사에서 준사관으로 임용된 사람은 제외한다)은 10년으로 하되, 임용된 날부터 7년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

6. 장기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 7년으로 한다. 다만, 대통령령으로 정하는 군의 필수 기술 분야에 종사하는 장기복무 부사관은 10년으로 하되, 장기복무 부사관으로 임용된 날부터 7년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

7. 단기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 4년으로 하되, 다음 각 목의 어느 하나에 해당하는 단기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 다음 각 목의 구분에 따른다.

가. 제6조제7항제3호의 단기복무 부사관: 「병역법」 제20조의2제1항에 따른 임기

나. 삭제 <2016. 12. 20.>

다. 제6조제7항제5호의 단기복무 부사관: 「병역법」 제18조 및 제19조에 따른 병의 복무기간

라. 제6조제7항제6호의 단기복무 부사관: 3년. 다만, 국방부장관은 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우에는 1년의 범위에서 그 복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

② 군인으로서 위탁교육이나 그 밖의 교육을 받은 사람은 다음 각 호의 구분에 따른 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산(加算)하여 복무한다. 이 경우 가산하여 복무할 기간은 의무복무 연한(年限) 내에 교육을 마친 경우에는 그 의무복무 연한 만료일의 다음 날부터 계산하고, 의무복무 연한이 지난 후에 교육을 마친 경우에는 그 교육이 끝난 날의 다음 날부터 계산한다. <개정 2023. 10. 31.>

1. 외국에서 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간의 2배에 상당하는 기간

2. 국내의 군 외의 교육기관에서 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간에 상당하는 기간

3. 국내의 군 교육기관에서 학위과정의 교육을 6개월 이상 받은 사람: 그 교육기간에 상당하는 기간

4. 국내에서 주간 근무를 하면서 일과 후 6개월 이상 또는 주말에 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간의 2분의 1에 상당하는 기간

③ 의무장교로서 기초의학과정이나 전문의학과정을 수습(修習)한 사람은 그 수습기간에 상당하는 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다.

④ 제62조제1항에 따라 선발되어 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 사람으로서 단기복무 장교로 임용된 사람은 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 기간에 상당하는 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다. 다만, 국방부장관은 제62조제1항에 따라 선발되어 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 사람으로서 부사관으로 임용된 사람에게는 그 의무복무기간에 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 기간 이내의 기간을 가산하여 복무하도록 할 수 있다. <개정 2012. 3. 21., 2017. 3. 21.>

⑤ 국방부장관은 특수장비를 운용하기 위하여 외국에서 위탁교육을 받은 사람에게는 다음 각 호의 구분에 따른 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무하도록 할 수 있다. 이 경우 그 가산 방법은 제2항에 따른다.

1. 그 이수기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간이 3년 미만인 경우: 3년까지

2. 그 이수기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간이 3년을 넘는 경우: 그 교육기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간

⑥ 제6조제4항 또는 제8항에 따라 전형을 거쳐 복무기간이 연장된 단기복무 장교 또는 단기복무 부사관은 그 연장된 복무기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다. <신설 2021. 4. 13.>

[전문개정 2011. 5. 24.]

<<군위탁생규정 제12조(지급경비의 반납조치)>> ①각군 참모총장은 군위탁생으로서 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 사람에 대해서는 제6조에 따라 지급받은 경비(이하 이 조에서 “지급경비”라 한다)를 별표의 기준에 따라 반납하도록 해야 하고, 본인이 반납하지 않는 경우에는 그의 보증인(「보험업법」에 따라 보증보험 증권을 발행한 보험회사를 포함한다. 이하 같다)에게 보증채무의 이행을 청구해야 한다. 다만, 지급경비의 환수가 곤란하거나 면제할 필요가 있을 때에는 각군 참모총장은 국방부장관의 승인(준사관 및 부사관의 경우는 제외한다)을 받아 반납을 6개월의 범위에서 연기하거나 그 일부 또는 전부의 반납을 면제할 수 있다. <개정 1995. 12. 22., 2001. 3. 27., 2019. 5. 28., 2021. 4. 20.>

1. 소정의 과정을 마친 후 정당한 사유 없이 복귀하지 아니한 사람

2. 수학 중 해임된 사람. 다만, 제10조제1항제1호(제5조제5호에 따른 결격사유로 한정한다) 또는 제11조에 해당하는 경우는 제외한다.

3. 소정의 과정을 마친 후 의무복무기간 중에 전역 또는 제적 등의 사유가 발생하여 복무의무를 이행하지 않은 사람

4. 교육결과보고서(제11조의2제3항에 따른 교육성과 자료를 포함한다. 이하 이 항에서 같다)의 내용이 교육목적을 달성하지 못한 것으로 평가된 사람

5. 다른 보고서 또는 논문 등을 표절하여 교육결과보고서를 제출한 사람

6. 교육결과보고서를 기한 내에 제출하지 못한 사람

7. 교육 과정이 학위 과정인 경우 학위를 취득하지 못한 사람

② 각군 참모총장은 제1항 각 호 외의 부분 본문에 따라 지급경비를 반납하게 할 경우에는 반납의무자에게 지급경비반납통고서를 보내야 한다. <개정 2019. 5. 28.>

③제1항 각 호 외의 부분 단서에 따라 지급경비의 반납을 연기하거나 면제받으려는 군위탁생 또는 그 보증인은 반납원인이 발생한 날부터 1개월 이내에 지급경비반납연기(면제)신청서를 소속군 참모총장에게 제출해야 한다. <신설 1995. 12. 22., 2021. 4. 20.>

④각군 참모총장은 반납의무자가 제2항의 규정에 의한 지급경비반납통고서를 받은 날 또는 제3항의 규정에 의한 반납연기기간이 끝난 날부터 90일이내에 지급경비를 납부하지 아니한 때에는 관할세무서장에게 이의 징수를 의뢰하여야 한다. <신설 1995. 12. 22.>

<<군위탁생규정 제12조의2(지급경비의 정산)>> ①각군 참모총장은 제6조의 규정에 의하여 지급한 경비에 대하여 정산사유가 발생한 때에는 관계증빙서류에 의하여 정산하여야 한다.

②제1항의 규정에 의한 정산에 관하여 필요한 사항은 국방부장관이 정한다.

[본조신설 1995. 12. 22.]

<<군위탁생규정  제6조(경비등의 지급)>> ①군위탁생에 대하여는 수학기간중 입학금ㆍ등록금 기타 필요한 경비를 지급한다.

②국외위탁생에 대하여는 왕복항공료 및 체재비를 지급하며, 6개월 이상 수학하는 국외위탁생에 대하여는 배우자 및 자녀의 왕복항공료, 의료보험료 또는 의료보조비, 생활준비금 및 귀국이전비를 가산하여 지급할 수 있다. 이 경우 체재비의 지급액은 월 단위로 계산하되, 월 미만의 일수에 대하여는 월 기준일을 30일로 하여 날 수에 비례하여 계산한다. <개정 2009. 10. 19.>

③군위탁생에 대한 제1항 및 제2항의 경비의 지급범위 및 지급액은 예산의 범위안에서 국방부장관이 정한다.

<<국가재정법 제96조(금전채권ㆍ채무의 소멸시효)>> ①금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리로서 시효에 관하여 다른 법률에 규정이 없는 것은 5년 동안 행사하지 아니하면 시효로 인하여 소멸한다.

②국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 제1항과 같다.

③금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리의 경우 소멸시효의 중단ㆍ정지 그 밖의 사항에 관하여 다른 법률의 규정이 없는 때에는 「민법」의 규정을 적용한다. 국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 같다. <개정 2020. 6. 9.>

④법령의 규정에 따라 국가가 행하는 납입의 고지는 시효중단의 효력이 있다.

<<민법 제166조(소멸시효의 기산점)>> ①소멸시효는 권리를 행사할 수 있는 때로부터 진행한다.

②부작위를 목적으로 하는 채권의 소멸시효는 위반행위를 한 때로부터 진행한다.

[단순위헌, 2014헌바148, 2018. 8. 30. 민법(1958. 2. 22. 법률 제471호로 제정된 것) 제166조 제1항 중 ‘진실ㆍ화해를 위한 과거사정리 기본법’ 제2조 제1항 제3호, 제4호에 규정된 사건에 적용되는 부분은 헌법에 위반된다.]


<<군 위탁교육 관리 훈령 제15조 (지급경비 정산)>> 지급경비 정산은 타 법령에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우를 제외하고는 아래 기준에 의거 정산한다.  

1. 체재비 

가. 체재비는 지급기간과 실제교육 기간(실제 출국일부터 귀국일까지를 말한다)의 차이가 5일 이하인 경우에는 환수하지 아니하고 6일 이상인 경우에는 5일을 차감한 후 일할 계산하여 환수한다. 

나. 체재비는 파견기간 기산일에 지급한다.

Rule 15c3-1 establishes minimum net capital requirements for broker-dealers to ensure financial stability and protect customer assets. 자본시장법 제172조(내부자의 단기매매차익 반환)
① 주권상장법인의 임원(「상법」 제401조의2제1항 각 호의 자를 포함한다. 이하 이 장에서 같다), 직원(직무상 제174조제1항의 미공개중요정보를 알 수 있는 자로서 대통령령으로 정하는 자에 한한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다) 또는 주요주주가 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 금융투자상품(이하 “특정증권등”이라 한다)을 매수(권리 행사의 상대방이 되는 경우로서 매수자의 지위를 가지게 되는 특정증권등의 매도를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)한 후 6개월 이내에 매도(권리를 행사할 수 있는 경우로서 매도자의 지위를 가지게 되는 특정증권등의 매수를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)하거나 특정증권등을 매도한 후 6개월 이내에 매수하여 이익을 얻은 경우에는 그 법인은 그 임직원 또는 주요주주에게 그 이익(이하 “단기매매차익”이라 한다)을 그 법인에게 반환할 것을 청구할 수 있다. 이 경우 이익의 산정기준·반환절차 등에 관하여 필요한 사항은 대통령령으로 정한다.

1. 그 법인이 발행한 증권(대통령령으로 정하는 증권을 제외한다)

2. 제1호의 증권과 관련된 증권예탁증권

3. 그 법인 외의 자가 발행한 것으로서 제1호 또는 제2호의 증권과 교환을 청구할 수 있는 교환사채권

4. 제1호부터 제3호까지의 증권만을 기초자산으로 하는 금융투자상품

자본시장법 제9조(그 밖의 용어의 정의) 
⑪ 이 법에서 “인수”란 제삼자에게 증권을 취득시킬 목적으로 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 행위를 하거나 그 행위를 전제로 발행인 또는 매출인을 위하여 증권의 모집·사모·매출을 하는 것을 말한다. <개정 2013. 5. 28.>

1. 그 증권의 전부 또는 일부를 취득하거나 취득하는 것을 내용으로 하는 계약을 체결하는 것

2. 그 증권의 전부 또는 일부에 대하여 이를 취득하는 자가 없는 때에 그 나머지를 취득하는 것을 내용으로 하는 계약을 체결하는 것

자본시장법 시행령 제198조(단기매매차익 반환의 예외) 법 제172조제6항에서 “대통령령으로 정하는 경우”란 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 경우를 말한다. <개정 2010. 12. 7., 2013. 8. 27., 2019. 6. 25.>
1. 법령에 따라 불가피하게 매수하거나 매도하는 경우

2. 정부의 허가ㆍ인가ㆍ승인 등이나 문서에 의한 지도ㆍ권고에 따라 매수하거나 매도하는 경우

3. 안정조작이나 시장조성을 위하여 매수ㆍ매도 또는 매도ㆍ매수하는 경우

4. 모집ㆍ사모ㆍ매출하는 특정증권등의 인수에 따라 취득하거나 인수한 특정증권등을 처분하는 경우

5. 주식매수선택권의 행사에 따라 주식을 취득하는 경우

6. 이미 소유하고 있는 지분증권, 신주인수권이 표시된 것, 전환사채권 또는 신주인수권부사채권의 권리행사에 따라 주식을 취득하는 경우

7. 법 제172조제1항제2호에 따른 증권예탁증권의 예탁계약 해지에 따라 법 제172조제1항제1호에 따른 증권을 취득하는 경우

8. 법 제172조제1항제1호에 따른 증권 중 제196조제1호라목에 따른 교환사채권 또는 법 제172조제1항제3호에 따른 교환사채권의 권리행사에 따라 증권을 취득하는 경우

9. 모집ㆍ매출하는 특정증권등의 청약에 따라 취득하는 경우

10. 「근로자복지기본법」 제32조에 따라 우리사주조합원에게 우선 배정된 주식의 청약에 따라 취득하는 경우

11. 주식매수청구권의 행사에 따라 주식을 처분하는 경우

12. 공개매수에 응모함에 따라 주식등을 처분하는 경우

13. 그 밖에 미공개중요정보를 이용할 염려가 없는 경우로서 증권선물위원회가 인정하는 경우

SOX Section 201 explicitly prohibits audit firms from providing nine categories of non-audit services (NAS) to their audit clients, including financial information systems design and implementation, actuarial services, and management functions. context:
The imperative for robust corporate governance, particularly concerning the independence and authority of the Chief Risk Officer (CRO), is a cornerstone of financial regulatory frameworks across leading global jurisdictions. In the United States, the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010 significantly bolstered requirements for risk management, mandating independent risk committees for certain financial institutions and emphasizing the CRO's critical role. Further guidance, such as OCC Bulletin 2010-42, outlines expectations for enterprise-wide risk management, underscoring that the CRO must possess sufficient stature, independence, and authority to effectively challenge business lines and report directly to the board or its risk committee. This structure implicitly supports a "Concurrent Position Prohibition" for the CRO, ensuring their focus remains solely on risk oversight without operational conflicts.

Similarly, within the European Union, comprehensive directives like MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) and CRD V (Directive 2019/878/EU) establish stringent organizational requirements for investment firms and credit institutions, respectively. Article 9 of MiFID II, for instance, requires firms to establish permanent and independent risk management functions. The EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05) further clarify that the risk management function, led by the CRO, must be independent from operational units and have sufficient resources. For an Asset Management Company, this means the CRO's role is to provide an objective assessment of investment risks, including those deliberated by an Investment Review Committee, without being directly involved in the committee's operational administration or decision-making processes beyond their risk advisory capacity. Such a prohibition on concurrent positions safeguards the integrity of the risk management framework, preventing situations where the CRO's oversight could be compromised by operational responsibilities. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) echo these principles through their Handbooks (e.g., SYSC 4.1.2), mandating clear segregation of duties and independence for control functions, reinforcing the global consensus on the CRO's distinct, non-conflicting mandate.

금융회사의 지배구조에 관한 법률 제28조(위험관리책임자의 임면 등) ① 금융회사(자산규모 및 영위하는 업무 등을 고려하여 대통령령으로 정하는 투자자문업자 및 투자일임업자는 제외한다)는 자산의 운용이나 업무의 수행, 그 밖의 각종 거래에서 발생하는 위험을 점검하고 관리하는 위험관리책임자를 1명 이상 두어야 한다.

In Asia, financial regulators also place a significant emphasis on the independence and authority of the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) within financial institutions, including Asset Management Companies. Singapore's Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), through its Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Financial Holding Companies, Banks, Direct Insurers and Reinsurers (e.g., section 4.1.1 on Risk Management Function), mandates that the risk management function must be adequately resourced, have sufficient authority, and operate independently of the business units. This framework inherently establishes a "Concurrent Position Prohibition" for the CRO, ensuring that their primary responsibility remains the objective identification, measurement, monitoring, and control of risks. The MAS expects the CRO to have direct access to the Board and senior management, enabling them to provide unvarnished risk assessments, particularly concerning investment decisions reviewed by an Investment Review Committee. Any involvement beyond providing independent risk analysis and challenge could be seen as compromising this critical independence.

Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) and its Corporate Governance Code similarly advocate for robust internal control systems and the clear segregation of duties. The FSA's Supervisory Guidelines for Financial Instruments Business Operators emphasize the need for effective risk management frameworks, where the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) plays a pivotal role in maintaining the integrity of the firm's risk profile. Principle 4 of Japan’s Corporate Governance Code encourages the establishment of an appropriate framework for effective internal control and risk management. For an Asset Management Company, this translates into ensuring the CRO's independence from front-office operations and administrative tasks related to investment decision-making bodies like the Investment Review Committee. The underlying principle across these jurisdictions is that the CRO's role is to challenge and oversee, not to administer or execute operational tasks that could dilute their objective risk perspective. Prohibiting concurrent positions that blur the lines between risk oversight and operational management is a fundamental safeguard for sound corporate governance and financial stability.

context:
The robust framework for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (CFT) compliance across leading global financial centers mandates stringent data retention policies for financial institutions. These policies are critical for supporting ongoing monitoring, facilitating investigations by competent authorities, and ensuring that institutions can demonstrate their adherence to regulatory obligations through comprehensive audit trails. The scope of data to be retained is extensive, encompassing all information gathered during the customer due diligence (CDD) process, transaction records, and internal analyses related to suspicious activity.

In the United States, the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), administered by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), establishes foundational requirements for financial institutions to maintain records. Specifically, 31 CFR Chapter X, which details FinCEN’s regulations, outlines various recordkeeping obligations. For instance, 31 CFR § 1010.430 requires financial institutions to retain records of certain funds transfers, while 31 CFR § 1020.220 mandates the establishment of a Customer Identification Program (CIP) that includes procedures for making and maintaining records of the information used to verify a customer's identity. Generally, these records, including those related to Currency Transaction Reports (CTRs), Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), and other BSA-mandated reports, must be retained for a period of five years. This five-year retention period typically commences from the date of the record's creation or, in the case of a SAR, from the date of filing. The purpose of this retention is multifaceted: it enables law enforcement agencies to trace illicit funds, provides a historical record for financial institutions to manage their AML/CFT risks, and serves as evidence of compliance during regulatory examinations. Financial institutions must ensure that these records are readily retrievable and securely stored, protecting them against unauthorized access or alteration, while also being accessible to regulators upon request.

Moving to the European Union, the framework is primarily governed by the Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2015/849, commonly known as 4AMLD), as amended by the Fifth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2018/843, 5AMLD). Article 40 of 4AMLD, titled 'Retention of documents and information,' explicitly addresses data retention requirements. It stipulates that Member States shall require obliged entities to retain the following documents and information: (a) documents and information obtained pursuant to the customer due diligence process, including copies of the identification documents or information equivalent to the copies, for a period of five years after the end of the business relationship with the customer or after the date of an occasional transaction; and (b) records of transactions, consisting of the original documents or copies admissible in court proceedings, for a period of five years after the carrying out of the transactions. The Directive further clarifies that after the expiry of the five-year period, Member States must ensure that obliged entities delete the personal data, unless otherwise provided for by national law, which determines under which circumstances obliged entities may or shall retain data for a longer period. Such longer retention periods are typically justified by the need for the prevention, detection, or investigation of money laundering or terrorist financing, and must be subject to appropriate safeguards. The 5AMLD introduced amendments to Article 40, emphasizing the need for robust data protection measures in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) while extending the scope to new obliged entities and enhancing beneficial ownership transparency. Financial institutions operating within the EU must therefore navigate the interplay between AML/CFT data retention requirements and strict data privacy regulations, ensuring that data is retained only for legitimate AML/CFT purposes and for the prescribed periods.

In the United Kingdom, the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on Payer) Regulations 2017 (MLRs 2017) transpose the EU AML Directives into national law, establishing comprehensive requirements for financial institutions and other obliged entities. Regulation 40, 'Retention of documents and information,' mirrors the provisions of the EU Directives. It mandates that relevant persons must keep: (a) a copy of the documents and information obtained for the purpose of customer due diligence measures; and (b) supporting records (consisting of the original documents or copies) in respect of a transaction which is subject to customer due diligence measures. The retention period specified is five years from the date on which the business relationship ends or the date on which the occasional transaction is completed. Regulation 41, 'Data protection,' further elaborates on the handling of retained data, particularly personal data. It states that personal data obtained for the purposes of these Regulations may only be processed for the prevention of money laundering or terrorist financing. It also stipulates that such data must not be retained for longer than is necessary for those purposes, with the five-year period serving as the general maximum unless a longer period is justified and proportionate to the prevention of money laundering or terrorist financing. Any retention beyond five years must be reviewed annually to determine if it remains necessary. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), as a primary supervisor for many financial institutions in the UK, provides detailed guidance on these regulations, emphasizing the need for robust record-keeping systems that allow for swift retrieval of information, proper identification of beneficial owners, and a clear audit trail of all CDD actions and transaction monitoring activities. The overall objective across these jurisdictions is to provide authorities with the necessary tools to investigate and prosecute financial crimes, while obliging financial institutions to act as gatekeepers through diligent record-keeping.

특정금융정보법 제5조의4(금융회사등의 금융거래등 정보의 보유기간 등) ① 금융회사등은 제4조, 제4조의2, 제5조의2 및 제5조의3에 따른 의무이행(이하 이 조에서 “의무이행”이라 한다)과 관련된 다음 각 호의 자료 및 정보를 금융거래등의 관계가 종료한 때부터 5년간 보존하여야 한다. <개정 2020. 3. 24.>

나. 보고 대상이 된 금융거래등 자료

다. 금융회사등이 제4조제3항에 따라 의심되는 합당한 근거를 기록한 자료

2. 제5조의2제1항 각 호에 따른 고객확인자료

3. 제5조의3제1항 각 호에 따른 송금인 및 수취인에 관한 정보

4. 그 밖에 의무이행과 관련하여 금융정보분석원장이 정하여 고시하는 자료

② 제1항 각 호 외의 부분에서 “금융거래등의 관계가 종료한 때”의 기준은 다음 각 호의 날로 한다. <개정 2020. 3. 24.>

1. 제2조제2호가목의 경우에는 금융회사등과 고객 사이에 모든 채권채무관계가 종료한 날

2. 제2조제2호나목에서 규정하는 파생상품시장에서의 거래의 경우에는 거래종료사유 발생으로 거래종료일이 도래한 날. 다만, 고객의 계좌가 개설되어 있는 경우에는 그 계좌가 폐쇄된 날로 본다.

3. 제2조제2호다목의 경우에는 카지노사업자와 고객 사이에 카지노거래로 인한 채권채무관계를 정산한 날

4. 제2조제2호라목의 경우에는 가상자산사업자와 고객 사이에 가상자산거래로 인한 채권채무관계를 정산한 날

5. 그 밖의 금융거래등의 경우에는 대통령령으로 정하는 날

③ 제1항에 따른 보존의 방법, 장소 등 그 밖에 필요한 사항은 대통령령으로 정한다.

자금세탁방지 및 공중협박자금조달금지에 관한 업무규정 제85조(보존대상) ① 금융회사등이 고객확인기록과 관련하여 보존해야 할 자료는 다음 각 호와 같다.

2. 고객신원정보 외에 금융거래의 목적 및 성격을 파악하기 위해 추가로 확인한 자료

개인정보보호법 제5조(국가 등의 책무) ① 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 목적 외 수집, 오용ㆍ남용 및 무분별한 감시ㆍ추적 등에 따른 폐해를 방지하여 인간의 존엄과 개인의 사생활 보호를 도모하기 위한 시책을 강구하여야 한다.

② 국가와 지방자치단체는 제4조에 따른 정보주체의 권리를 보호하기 위하여 법령의 개선 등 필요한 시책을 마련하여야 한다.

③ 국가와 지방자치단체는 만 14세 미만 아동이 개인정보 처리가 미치는 영향과 정보주체의 권리 등을 명확하게 알 수 있도록 만 14세 미만 아동의 개인정보 보호에 필요한 시책을 마련하여야 한다. <신설 2023. 3. 14.>

④ 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 처리에 관한 불합리한 사회적 관행을 개선하기 위하여 개인정보처리자의 자율적인 개인정보 보호활동을 존중하고 촉진ㆍ지원하여야 한다. <개정 2023. 3. 14.>

⑤ 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 처리에 관한 법령 또는 조례를 적용할 때에는 정보주체의 권리가 보장될 수 있도록 개인정보 보호 원칙에 맞게 적용하여야 한다. <개정 2023. 3. 14.>

② 개인정보처리자는 정보주체의 동의를 받아 개인정보를 수집하는 경우 필요한 최소한의 정보 외의 개인정보 수집에는 동의하지 아니할 수 있다는 사실을 구체적으로 알리고 개인정보를 수집하여야 한다. <신설 2013. 8. 6.>

③ 개인정보처리자는 정보주체가 필요한 최소한의 정보 외의 개인정보 수집에 동의하지 아니한다는 이유로 정보주체에게 재화 또는 서비스의 제공을 거부하여서는 아니 된다. <개정 2013. 8. 6.>

Beyond the transatlantic regulatory landscapes, other prominent financial hubs globally have also established rigorous AML/CFT data retention requirements, often drawing inspiration from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Recommendations, which serve as the international standard. These jurisdictions ensure that financial institutions maintain comprehensive records to facilitate investigations, support ongoing risk assessments, and demonstrate compliance with national and international obligations. The emphasis remains on the retention of customer due diligence (CDD) information, transaction records, and any internal analyses related to suspicious activities.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issues specific notices to financial institutions outlining their AML/CFT obligations. For banks, MAS Notice 626, titled 'Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Banks,' is a cornerstone. Paragraph 11 of MAS Notice 626 details the record-keeping requirements. It mandates that a bank must keep records, for a period of at least five years, of: (a) all transactions, both domestic and international; (b) the information obtained through its CDD measures; and (c) any reports made to the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO). The five-year retention period commences from the date on which the business relationship with the customer is terminated, or, in the case of an occasional transaction, from the date of the transaction. For transactions that do not form part of a business relationship, the five-year period runs from the date of the transaction. The Notice specifies that records must be sufficient to permit the reconstruction of individual transactions and to provide evidence for the prosecution of criminal activity. This includes, but is not limited to, copies of identification documents, account files, business correspondence, and transaction records such as payment orders, swift messages, and account statements. Furthermore, banks are expected to maintain records in a manner that allows for timely retrieval by the MAS or other competent authorities. The MAS places a strong emphasis on the integrity and security of these records, requiring banks to implement appropriate measures to protect against unauthorized access, alteration, or destruction. The overarching goal is to ensure that a comprehensive audit trail exists for all financial activities, enabling effective oversight and enforcement against money laundering and terrorist financing. Compliance with these data retention provisions is a critical component of a bank's overall AML/CFT framework, subject to regular inspection and audit by the MAS.

In Japan, the Financial Services Agency (FSA) oversees the implementation of AML/CFT measures, primarily based on the Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds (APTCP). While the APTCP sets out the core legal framework, the FSA issues detailed guidelines and supervisory policies for various financial sectors, including banks, securities firms, and insurance companies. These guidelines often elaborate on the requirements for customer identification, transaction monitoring, and record-keeping, aligning with FATF Recommendations. Japanese financial institutions are generally required to retain records relating to customer identification and transaction details for a minimum of seven to ten years. Specifically, under the APTCP and related ordinances, financial institutions must retain the following types of information: (a) customer identification data, including copies of identification documents, for seven years from the termination of the business relationship; and (b) transaction records, including transaction details, for seven years from the date of the transaction. For certain types of records, such as those pertaining to suspicious transactions or complex transactions, the retention period may be extended or subject to specific requirements. The purpose of these extended retention periods, compared to the standard five years in some other jurisdictions, is to provide a longer historical view for investigative bodies to trace complex financial crimes, which often span multiple years. The FSA's guidelines emphasize the need for financial institutions to implement robust systems for managing and archiving these records, ensuring their accuracy, completeness, and accessibility. This includes maintaining records of the beneficial ownership information obtained during the CDD process, which is crucial for uncovering illicit financial networks. The records must be kept in a manner that allows them to be easily retrieved and presented to supervisory authorities or law enforcement agencies upon request. Furthermore, Japanese regulations often require financial institutions to retain records of their internal analyses and decisions regarding suspicious transactions, providing a transparent audit trail of their AML/CFT compliance efforts. The stringent data retention requirements in Japan underscore a commitment to combating financial crime by ensuring that a thorough historical record is available to support enforcement actions and regulatory oversight, thereby strengthening the integrity of the financial system against the threats of money laundering and terrorist financing.

context:
Regulatory frameworks across leading financial jurisdictions frequently impose stringent limitations on the equity investments made by financial institutions, primarily to safeguard financial stability, prevent undue concentration of power, and mitigate systemic risk. In the United States, for instance, the **Investment Company Act of 1940** (15 U.S.C. § 80a-1 et seq.) contains provisions designed to regulate investment companies and, indirectly, to influence how other financial entities interact with them. Specifically, **Section 12(d)** of the Act outlines restrictions on the acquisition of shares of other investment companies by registered investment companies. While primarily aimed at preventing fund-of-funds abuses, the underlying principle of preventing excessive control or complex ownership structures resonates across broader regulatory concerns regarding institutional investments. Furthermore, the **Bank Holding Company Act of 1956** (12 U.S.C. § 1841 et seq.) and its implementing regulations, such as the Federal Reserve Board’s **Regulation Y** (12 CFR Part 225), significantly restrict the non-banking activities and equity investments of bank holding companies and their subsidiaries. These rules generally limit a bank holding company’s ability to own or control more than 5% of the voting shares of a company engaged in activities not deemed “closely related to banking,” requiring prior Federal Reserve approval for certain acquisitions or investments that exceed specified thresholds or result in control. This framework is crucial for maintaining the separation of banking and commerce and for ensuring that taxpayer-backed financial institutions do not engage in excessively speculative or risky ventures. A more recent and prominent example is the **Volcker Rule**, codified in **Section 619 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act** (12 U.S.C. § 1851). This rule prohibits banking entities from engaging in proprietary trading and from acquiring or retaining any equity, partnership, or other ownership interest in, or sponsoring, a hedge fund or private equity fund, subject to certain exceptions. The Volcker Rule directly addresses concerns about financial institutions taking on excessive risk through speculative investments, thereby protecting the stability of the financial system. 

In the European Union, the **Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR)** (Regulation (EU) No 575/2013) and the **Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV)** (Directive 2013/36/EU), now updated by **CRR II** (Regulation (EU) 2019/876) and **CRD V** (Directive (EU) 2019/878), establish prudential requirements for credit institutions and investment firms. These instruments contain rules on large exposures and qualifying holdings, which directly impact a financial institution's ability to make significant equity investments in other entities. For instance, Article 395 of the CRR sets limits on large exposures, generally restricting an institution’s exposure to a single client or group of connected clients to 25% of its eligible capital. While not solely focused on equity, this can limit the size of a controlling or substantial equity stake. Furthermore, Article 46 of the CRR outlines deductions from Common Equity Tier 1 capital for certain holdings, including significant investments in other financial sector entities, effectively discouraging excessive cross-holdings. The **Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD)** (Directive 2011/61/EU) regulates managers of alternative investment funds (AIFs) and, while primarily focused on the management of third-party assets, it indirectly influences investment strategies and risk management practices, including potential limits on leverage and certain types of investments, especially when prudential regulators assess the overall risk profile of a financial institution that also operates as an AIFM. 

The United Kingdom, post-Brexit, largely retains similar principles through the **FCA Handbook** and **PRA Rulebook**. The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) imposes specific rules on banks, building societies, and insurers, including requirements for capital adequacy and limits on large exposures. For insurers, **Solvency II** (retained EU law framework, now implemented via the PRA Rulebook) imposes detailed requirements on the valuation of assets and liabilities, own funds, and capital requirements, including specific rules on asset allocation and diversification. These rules inherently constrain the types and concentrations of equity investments insurers can make to ensure policyholder protection and financial stability. For example, the PRA's **Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)** requires firms to assess their own risks, including concentration risks arising from large equity holdings, and to hold adequate capital against them. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) also maintains rules under its **Conduct of Business Sourcebook (COBS)** and **Systems and Controls (SYSC)**, which, while focusing on investor protection and governance, indirectly influence the types of investments financial institutions can undertake by demanding robust risk management and due diligence processes. The UK’s regulatory approach consistently emphasizes the need for financial institutions to manage their investment exposures prudently, preventing concentrations that could pose risks to their solvency or the broader financial system.

While the PSA does not explicitly detail the assignability of underlying receivables from merchant transactions, it establishes the regulatory environment for how payment service providers manage, settle, and secure funds, indirectly influencing the nature and transferability of claims held by and against them. The FSA's regulatory framework prioritizes the transparency of payment flows and the security of transactions, ensuring that even if underlying financial claims are transferred or securitized, customer funds remain adequately protected and accessible.

context:
Under the European Union's Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU), investment firms are subject to stringent requirements for the safeguarding of client assets, particularly for retail investors engaging in foreign securities transactions. Article 16(8) mandates firms to make adequate arrangements to safeguard clients’ ownership rights and prevent the use of client financial instruments for their own account. Similarly, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Client Assets Sourcebook (CASS) rules, specifically CASS 7, outline detailed obligations for firms holding client money and safe custody assets. In the United States, SEC Rule 15c3-3 (Customer Protection - Reserves and Custody of Securities) requires broker-dealers to maintain physical possession or control over customers' fully paid and excess margin securities. The 'delivery out' or transfer of foreign securities from a domestic investment firm to a foreign brokerage, initiated by a retail investor, necessitates adherence to these protective frameworks, ensuring proper record-keeping and minimizing operational risks during the transfer process.

자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률 시행령 제184조(해외시장 거래 등) ① 법 제166조에 따라 일반투자자(금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 전문투자자를 포함한다)는 해외 증권시장이나 해외 파생상품시장에서 외화증권 및 장내파생상품의 매매거래(외국 다자간매매체결회사에서의 거래를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)를 하려는 경우에는 투자중개업자를 통하여 매매거래를 해야 한다. 다만, 외화증권을 매도하려는 경우로서 다음 각 호의 요건을 모두 충족하는 경우에는 투자중개업자를 통하지 않고 매매거래를 할 수 있다. <개정 2013. 8. 27., 2021. 2. 9., 2024. 3. 5.>

1. 투자매매업자를 상대방으로 하거나 투자중개업자를 통하여 취득한 외화증권이 아닐 것

2. 외화증권의 취득이 「외국환거래법」 제18조제1항 단서에 따라 신고의무가 면제되는 자본거래로서 금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 거래에 해당할 것

외국환거래법 제18조(자본거래의 신고 등) ① 자본거래를 하려는 자는 대통령령으로 정하는 바에 따라 재정경제부장관에게 신고하여야 한다. 다만, 외국환수급 안정과 대외거래 원활화를 위하여 대통령령으로 정하는 자본거래는 사후에 보고하거나 신고하지 아니할 수 있다. <개정 2017. 1. 17., 2025. 10. 1.>

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) under its Securities and Futures Act (SFA) and subsidiary legislation, such as the Securities and Futures (Capital Markets) Regulations, imposes robust requirements on investment firms for the segregation and protection of client assets. Part VI of these regulations specifies conditions for holding client money and assets, ensuring that foreign securities held for retail investors are identifiable and protected from claims by the firm's creditors. In Japan, the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA) mandates similar strict segregation rules, requiring financial instruments business operators to keep client assets separate from their own, thereby safeguarding retail investors' foreign securities. The process of 'delivery out' or transferring these foreign securities from a domestic investment firm to an overseas brokerage is subject to these regulatory frameworks, which prioritize client asset integrity and operational transparency. Firms must ensure that such transfers comply with anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing obligations in both jurisdictions, as well as cross-border reporting requirements.

In the United States, robust governance structures for risk management are mandated across various financial sectors, emphasizing independence and accountability. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX), while primarily focused on financial reporting and corporate governance for public companies, underpins the broader principle of independent oversight that extends to risk management functions. For banking institutions, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) Handbook on Corporate Governance and Enterprise Risk Management frequently stresses the imperative for a chief risk officer (CRO), often analogous to a Risk Management Officer (위험관리책임자), to possess sufficient authority and independence from revenue-generating lines of business. This often implies strict limitations on Concurrent Duties (겸직 금지) that could create conflicts of interest, particularly concerning operational functions like Loan Review or credit origination. The CRO is typically expected to report to the board or a dedicated risk committee, ensuring separation from executive management responsible for business generation. 

Similarly, within the European Union, the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU) and its accompanying delegated regulations impose stringent organisational requirements on investment firms. Article 22 of MiFID II, supplemented by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 (Article 21), mandates that firms establish and maintain a permanent and effective risk management function that is functionally independent from the operational units. This functional independence explicitly requires that the Risk Management Officer (위험관리책임자) or the risk management function's personnel are not involved in the performance of the functions they monitor. Engagement in activities such as direct Loan Review decisions or investment portfolio management is generally considered a breach of this independence requirement, constituting a prohibited form of Concurrent Duties (겸직 금지). The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) echoes these principles through its Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls (SYSC) handbook, particularly SYSC 6 (Compliance and internal audit) and SYSC 7 (Risk control). Under the UK's Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), specific responsibilities are assigned to Senior Managers, including those responsible for risk, reinforcing the need for clear lines of accountability and the avoidance of conflicts arising from Concurrent Duties (겸직 금지) that could compromise the integrity of the risk management function, especially in areas like Loan Review.

라. 보험계약 인수에 관한 업무

마. 보험계약 관리에 관한 업무

바. 보험금 지급에 관한 업무

The head of this division, acting as the Risk Management Officer (위험관리책임자), is expected to oversee and report on the institution's overall risk profile without being directly involved in profit-generating activities. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and major stock exchanges like the NYSE and NASDAQ have established stringent corporate governance requirements for publicly listed financial companies. For instance, NYSE Listed Company Manual Section 303A.01 mandates that listed companies must have a majority of independent directors. Furthermore, Section 303A.03 requires that non-management directors meet at regularly scheduled executive sessions without management. While not strictly mandated by federal law, the role of a Lead Independent Director is often adopted, particularly when the roles of Board chairperson and CEO are combined, to provide an independent counterweight and leadership for the non-executive directors. This structure enhances the independent oversight function of the board, crucial for robust corporate governance.

Across the Atlantic, the United Kingdom's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) supervises financial institutions, often referencing the UK Corporate Governance Code (issued by the Financial Reporting Council, FRC). Principle J of the Code emphasizes that the roles of chair and chief executive should not be exercised by the same individual to ensure a clear division of responsibilities and to promote a balance of power. The Code also advocates for a strong non-executive director presence, including a Senior Independent Director, who serves as a crucial point of contact for shareholders and acts as a sounding board for the Board chairperson. This framework aims to bolster the effectiveness of corporate governance within financial companies, ensuring accountability and strategic oversight.

The European Union's regulatory landscape for financial companies, particularly under the Capital Requirements Directive V (CRD V, Directive (EU) 2019/878 amending Directive 2013/36/EU), places significant emphasis on the suitability and composition of management bodies. Article 88 of CRD V requires institutions to have a sufficient number of non-executive directors and independent directors on their boards, ensuring a broad range of experience and an appropriate level of independence. It also mandates that the management body define and oversee the implementation of the institution’s governance arrangements, including the separation of duties and prevention of conflicts of interest, thereby reinforcing the overall corporate governance framework.

The MAS Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Banks (e.g., paragraph 3.4.1) stipulate that the board should comprise a majority of independent directors, particularly for locally-incorporated banks. Where the Board chairperson is not independent or where the roles of chairman and CEO are combined, the appointment of a Lead Independent Director is strongly encouraged. The Lead Independent Director serves as a principal independent point of contact for shareholders and provides leadership to the non-executive directors, enhancing independent oversight.

The Code, first introduced in 2015 and revised periodically (e.g., in 2021), emphasizes the appointment of at least two independent outside directors for listed companies, including financial companies, to strengthen the board's oversight function and ensure greater transparency. Principle 4.8 of the Code specifically addresses the roles of independent directors in overseeing management and engaging with stakeholders. While the Code does not strictly mandate the separation of the Board chairperson and CEO roles, it encourages companies to consider the appropriate balance and to clearly define the responsibilities of the Board chairperson in fostering effective board discussions and decision-making. The overarching goal is to enhance the long-term corporate value and sustainable growth of financial companies through effective corporate governance.

The global financial landscape is characterized by an intricate web of regulatory requirements designed to safeguard consumer data, ensure market integrity, and combat illicit financial activities. In the United States, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) stands as a foundational pillar for financial privacy, mandating that financial institutions explain their information-sharing practices to customers and protect sensitive data. Specifically, the GLBA's Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) requires financial institutions to implement comprehensive information security programs to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of nonpublic personal information (NPI). This includes establishing administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer records and information. Such NPI often encompasses detailed financial transaction information and personal credit information, the handling of which is meticulously prescribed. Furthermore, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) enforces Regulation S-P, 'Privacy of Consumer Financial Information' (17 CFR Part 248), which applies to broker-dealers, investment companies, and investment advisers. Regulation S-P mirrors many GLBA provisions, requiring these entities to adopt policies and procedures to protect customer records and information, and to provide privacy notices to customers. The ongoing evolution of cyber threats has also led to state-level regulations, such as the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500). This regulation imposes stringent cybersecurity requirements on financial institutions operating in New York, including risk assessments, multi-factor authentication, incident response plans, and a notification duty for cybersecurity events. These frameworks collectively emphasize robust data governance, access controls, and encryption to shield customer data from unauthorized access or misuse, even in scenarios involving potential requests from governmental bodies under tax laws, where the scope and legality of such data sharing are carefully scrutinized against privacy protections.

Across the Atlantic, the European Union's regulatory framework is dominated by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a comprehensive data protection law that sets a high bar for the processing of personal data, including financial transaction information and personal credit information. GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) applies extraterritorially, impacting any entity processing data of EU residents. Article 5 outlines core data processing principles, including lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, and confidentiality. Article 6 specifies the lawful bases for processing, such as consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, or legitimate interests. When governmental bodies, akin to a National Tax Service, seek financial transaction information under national tax laws, financial institutions must ensure such requests align with a valid legal obligation under Article 6(1)(c) or a public interest task under Article 6(1)(e), and that the disclosure is proportionate and necessary. Article 32 mandates appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, while Articles 33 and 34 establish a strict notification duty for data breaches, requiring prompt reporting to supervisory authorities and, in high-risk cases, to affected data subjects. The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), alongside its accompanying Regulation (MiFIR), while primarily focused on market transparency and investor protection, indirectly imposes significant data management requirements. MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) Article 16 mandates robust organizational requirements for investment firms, including systems and controls for data recording and storage, particularly for client orders and transactions. Article 25 further specifies extensive record-keeping obligations for all services, transactions, and communications, generating vast quantities of financial transaction information that subsequently fall under GDPR's protective umbrella. The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), effective from 2025, will further enhance the EU's financial sector resilience against ICT-related disruptions and threats. DORA mandates comprehensive ICT risk management frameworks, incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing, and robust third-party risk management, all of which directly bolster the security and integrity of financial transaction information and personal credit information held by financial entities. The interaction between these regulations means that any request for data, even for tax purposes, must navigate a complex interplay of privacy, security, and operational resilience requirements.

In the United Kingdom, following its departure from the EU, the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 largely mirror the EU GDPR's provisions, maintaining a high standard for personal data protection. Financial institutions are subject to the same principles of lawfulness, fairness, and transparency for processing personal credit information and financial transaction information, including when responding to requests from HMRC (Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs) under specific tax laws. The notification duty for data breaches remains a critical compliance obligation, with reporting to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and affected individuals as required. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Handbook also imposes significant requirements through its Principles for Businesses (PRIN) and Systems and Controls (SYSC) chapters. PRIN 3 requires firms to take reasonable care to organize and control their affairs responsibly and effectively, with adequate risk management systems, which inherently includes data protection. SYSC 8, in particular, focuses on information security, requiring firms to establish, implement, and maintain adequate policies and procedures sufficient to ensure the security, integrity, and confidentiality of information. This extends to the secure handling of financial transaction information and personal credit information, ensuring that even legitimate requests, for example, from the National Tax Service equivalent under tax laws, are processed with appropriate safeguards and recorded diligently. The Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), while primarily focusing on individual accountability, indirectly reinforces data governance by assigning clear responsibilities for risk management and control functions, including those related to data protection and cybersecurity, ensuring that senior leadership is accountable for the firm's compliance with these stringent data handling requirements and the timely execution of any notification duty.

In Singapore, the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) 2012 provides a comprehensive data protection regime applicable to all organizations, including financial institutions, handling personal data. The PDPA establishes nine key obligations: Consent, Purpose Limitation, Notification, Access and Correction, Accuracy, Protection, Retention Limitation, Transfer Limitation, and Accountability. Sections 13 to 16, specifically, require organizations to obtain consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of personal data, including financial transaction information and personal credit information, and to ensure that such processing is for reasonable purposes. This means that even when a governmental body, analogous to a National Tax Service, seeks data under specific tax laws, financial institutions must ensure that the disclosure aligns with one of the PDPA's exceptions to consent (e.g., for legal or regulatory requirements) and adheres to the purpose limitation principle. Section 24 of the PDPA outlines the mandatory notification duty in the event of a data breach, requiring organizations to assess the breach and, if it is notifiable, to inform the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) and affected individuals without undue delay. Furthermore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issues detailed Technology Risk Management (TRM) Guidelines, which set out expectations for financial institutions to manage technology risks, including cybersecurity and data protection. The MAS TRM Guidelines emphasize the need for robust information security measures, data integrity, and resilience against cyber threats, directly impacting how financial transaction information and personal credit information are stored, processed, and transmitted. These guidelines mandate regular risk assessments, implementation of strong access controls, encryption, and comprehensive incident response plans, ensuring that data is protected throughout its lifecycle, even when subject to requests under tax laws, thereby reinforcing the institution's notification duty to regulators and affected parties in case of security incidents.

The APPI (Act No. 57 of 2003) sets forth fundamental principles for the handling of personal information, including explicit provisions for financial institutions. Article 15 mandates that personal information, including sensitive financial transaction information and personal credit information, must be handled within the scope necessary to achieve a specified purpose of use. Article 17 requires entities to acquire personal information by appropriate means and not through deception or other illicit methods. Critically, Article 20 obliges organizations to take necessary and appropriate measures for the security management of personal data, including preventing leakage, loss, or damage, and for the supervision of employees and contractors handling such data. This is particularly relevant when a governmental body, akin to a National Tax Service, requests financial information under tax laws; the disclosure must align with an exception or a specific legal mandate that overrides the consent requirement, and the institution must document the legal basis meticulously. In the event of a data breach, Article 26 and related guidelines establish a notification duty to the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) and, in certain circumstances, to the affected data subjects, ensuring transparency and accountability. The FSA, as the primary regulator for financial institutions, issues comprehensive guidelines for the supervision of various financial business operators, which often elaborate on the APPI's requirements within the financial context. These guidelines emphasize the importance of robust internal control systems for information security management, including systems for preventing unauthorized access, ensuring data accuracy, and maintaining business continuity. The regulatory landscape for financial institutions across major global jurisdictions consistently emphasizes robust corporate governance, particularly concerning the concurrent positions held by executives and directors. This focus stems from the imperative to mitigate conflicts of interest, ensure sufficient time commitment, maintain independence, and prevent anti-competitive practices. Jurisdictions such as the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom have developed intricate frameworks to address these concerns.

In the United States, the prevention of interlocking directorates, where the same person serves as a director or officer for multiple competing financial institutions, is a cornerstone of antitrust law. Section 8 of the Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. § 19) explicitly prohibits such interlocks between certain competing corporations, particularly those engaged in commerce. This prohibition is further elaborated and enforced by the Federal Reserve Board through its Regulation L (12 CFR Part 212), which applies to depository institutions. Regulation L specifies conditions under which an individual may serve as an officer or director of more than one depository organization and outlines exceptions, such as those for affiliated organizations or organizations not deemed 'competitors' under the statutory definition. The primary objective is to prevent concentrated power and information sharing that could lead to reduced competition. Beyond antitrust concerns, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and major stock exchanges like the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and NASDAQ impose stringent independence requirements for directors of listed companies, particularly for those serving on audit committees. For instance, Exchange Act Rule 10A-3 mandates that audit committee members be independent, prohibiting them from receiving any consulting, advisory, or other compensatory fee from the issuer or its subsidiaries, or being an affiliated person of the issuer. While not directly limiting the number of concurrent positions, the spirit of independence and the expectation of sufficient time commitment are inherent in these rules.

The European Union has significantly strengthened its corporate governance requirements for financial institutions, particularly through the Capital Requirements Directive V (CRD V, Directive (EU) 2019/878). Article 88 of CRD V, pertaining to the 'management body', introduces specific limits on the number of directorships that members of the management body of a financial institution may hold concurrently. For significant financial institutions, an individual may hold either one executive directorship and two non-executive directorships, or four non-executive directorships. These limits are designed to ensure that members of the management body can dedicate sufficient time to their responsibilities within the financial institution. Member States have the discretion to allow one additional non-executive directorship where the non-executive directorships are held in companies that are not financial undertakings. The European Banking Authority (EBA) further elaborates on these provisions through its 'Guidelines on internal governance' (EBA/GL/2021/05), which provide detailed guidance on the assessment of suitability, including the time commitment required for members of the management body and the management of actual or potential conflicts of interest arising from concurrent positions.

In the United Kingdom, following its departure from the EU, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) maintain a robust regulatory framework that largely aligns with the principles of CRD V and MiFID II. The Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), established under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) and implemented through the PRA Rulebook and FCA Handbook, places a strong emphasis on individual accountability, fitness, and propriety. While the UK does not always impose explicit numerical limits on concurrent directorships for all executives, the 'fitness and propriety' assessment for senior managers (as outlined in SYSC 5.1 and the PRA/FCA Statements of Principle and Code of Conduct for Senior Managers) inherently considers whether an individual has sufficient time, capacity, and integrity to perform their designated responsibilities effectively. Any concurrent position that could lead to a conflict of interest or compromise an individual's ability to dedicate adequate time to their primary role in a financial institution would be scrutinized under these rules. The FCA Handbook's SYSC 10 (Conflicts of Interest) also mandates firms to take all reasonable steps to identify, prevent, manage, and disclose conflicts of interest, which would include those potentially arising from executives holding positions in other entities.

These jurisdictions often blend statutory requirements with comprehensive corporate governance codes and supervisory guidelines to ensure sound oversight and ethical conduct.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) plays a central role in regulating financial institutions and promoting strong corporate governance practices. The MAS Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Financial Holding Companies, Banks, Direct Insurers, and Reinsurers (e.g., MAS 604, MAS 605, MAS 606, and corresponding notices) set forth detailed expectations for the boards of directors and senior management. These guidelines emphasize the importance of director independence and the management of conflicts of interest. While not imposing strict numerical limits on all concurrent positions, the guidelines stress that directors should have sufficient time to discharge their duties effectively. Principle 4 of the Singapore Code of Corporate Governance (issued by MAS and the Singapore Exchange Regulation, SGX RegCo), which applies to listed companies, addresses board composition and the capacity of directors. Guidance 4.3 of the Code states that the Nomination Committee should review and determine the maximum number of listed company board representations that any director may hold, and should take into account the director’s other principal commitments. This ensures that directors, particularly independent directors, are not over-committed and can dedicate adequate attention to their responsibilities. Furthermore, the Banking Act and the Securities and Futures Act (SFA) contain provisions that empower MAS to assess the fitness and propriety of directors and senior management, which includes considering any potential conflicts arising from concurrent roles.

Japan’s financial regulatory landscape, overseen by the Financial Services Agency (FSA) and influenced by the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE), places significant emphasis on corporate governance, particularly for listed financial institutions. The Corporate Governance Code, jointly issued by the FSA and TSE, provides a set of principles and guidelines for companies to enhance their governance structures. Principle 4.1 of the Code encourages companies to ensure effective functioning of the board of directors, including the appointment of independent outside directors. Supplementary Principle 4.1.3 explicitly states that companies should disclose the significant concurrent positions of their directors and corporate auditors, and for independent outside directors, the board should ensure that they secure sufficient time to fulfill their duties. While the Code does not prescribe a specific numerical limit for concurrent positions, it mandates transparency and an internal assessment of time commitment and potential conflicts. The FSA’s supervisory guidelines for banking groups and financial conglomerates often reinforce these expectations, requiring financial institutions to establish robust internal control frameworks to manage conflicts of interest, including those arising from executives holding positions in other entities. The Banking Act and the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA) provide the statutory basis for these governance requirements, empowering the FSA to ensure the sound management and effective oversight of financial institutions. The protection of client financial data is a cornerstone of regulatory frameworks across global financial markets, with robust provisions implemented to ensure confidentiality, prevent unauthorized disclosure, and mandate explicit consent for specific data uses. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) enforces Regulation S-P (17 CFR § 248.1 et seq.), which governs the privacy of consumer financial information held by financial institutions. Specifically, Rule 4 of Regulation S-P requires financial institutions to provide their customers with a clear and conspicuous notice that accurately reflects their privacy policies and practices. This notice must explain the types of nonpublic personal information the institution collects, the categories of affiliates and nonaffiliated third parties to whom the institution may disclose such information, and the categories of information it discloses. Furthermore, Rule 7 mandates that financial institutions provide customers with an opportunity to opt out before the institution discloses nonpublic personal information to nonaffiliated third parties, subject to certain exceptions. This opt-out mechanism is a critical component of ensuring customer control over their data, defining the permissible scope of information sharing. The safeguarding of customer records and information is also addressed under Rule 30 of Regulation S-P, requiring institutions to adopt policies and procedures reasonably designed to protect the security and confidentiality of customer records and information, and to protect against unauthorized access to or use of such records or information that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer. This extends beyond mere disclosure to encompass the integrity and resilience of data storage and processing systems.

In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR - Regulation (EU) 2016/679) sets a comprehensive standard for data protection, significantly impacting financial services firms. Article 5 of the GDPR outlines key principles for processing personal data, including lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, and confidentiality. Consent, as a legal basis for processing, is rigorously defined under Article 4(11) and elaborated upon in Article 7, requiring it to be freely given, specific, informed, and an unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by a statement or by a clear affirmative action. Article 7(2) further specifies that if consent is given in the context of a written declaration, it must be clearly distinguishable from other matters, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language. This stringent requirement directly impacts how financial institutions obtain and manage customer permissions for processing 'transaction information, etc.' and other personal data, ensuring that the 'scope of information' covered by consent is explicit and understood. For special categories of personal data (e.g., health data potentially relevant to certain insurance products), Article 9 imposes even stricter conditions, generally prohibiting processing unless explicit consent is obtained or specific derogations apply. Moreover, MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU and Regulation (EU) No 600/2014) complements GDPR by imposing specific obligations on investment firms regarding client information. Article 24(4) of MiFID II requires firms to obtain from clients the necessary information regarding their knowledge and experience, financial situation, and investment objectives to assess suitability or appropriateness. This 'transaction information, etc.' is then protected under GDPR, emphasizing the 'confidentiality' aspect. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) mirrors these principles in its Handbook, particularly in the Principles for Businesses (PRIN) and Conduct of Business Sourcebook (COBS), upholding the need for firms to act with integrity and treat customers fairly, which inherently includes robust data protection and confidentiality. For instance, Principle 2 (Skill, care and diligence) and Principle 10 (Customers' assets) underscore the responsibility for safeguarding client data, while COBS 2.2.1R requires firms to act honestly, fairly and professionally in accordance with the best interests of its clients, which extends to the handling of their financial information and consent for its use, ensuring 'confidentiality' and defining the 'scope of information' shared with the 'consent of the account holder'.

The robust architecture of international financial regulation places paramount importance on the internal governance, risk management, and compliance frameworks of regulated entities. Across major jurisdictions such as the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, stringent requirements are imposed on financial institutions to establish and maintain robust oversight mechanisms, often necessitating the appointment of highly qualified personnel in supervisory and control functions. These frameworks aim to safeguard market integrity, protect consumers, and ensure the sound operation of financial markets.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) mandate comprehensive compliance programs for investment advisers and broker-dealers. For instance, under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, specifically Rule 206(4)-7, registered investment advisers are required to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder. A critical component of this rule is the designation of a Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) who is responsible for administering the compliance policies and procedures. While the rule does not explicitly detail specific academic qualifications, the SEC emphasizes that the CCO must be competent and knowledgeable regarding the Advisers Act and the firm's operations. The expectation is that the CCO possesses sufficient legal or industry experience to effectively discharge their duties, including conducting annual reviews of the adequacy of the firm’s compliance policies and procedures and the effectiveness of their implementation. Similarly, FINRA Rule 3110, relating to Supervision, requires member firms to establish and maintain a system to supervise the activities of each registered representative, registered principal, and other associated person that is reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations. This necessitates the appointment of appropriately qualified supervisory principals, whose experience and knowledge must be commensurate with the scope and complexity of the activities they supervise.

The European Union, through its Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), codified in Directive 2014/65/EU, sets out detailed organizational requirements for investment firms. Article 16 of MiFID II, focusing on organizational requirements, mandates that investment firms establish, implement, and maintain adequate policies and procedures sufficient to ensure compliance of the firm, including its managers, employees, and tied agents, with its obligations under MiFID II and relevant national law. This includes requirements for a permanent and effective compliance function, independent risk management function, and internal audit function. Specifically, Article 16(2) requires firms to employ personnel with the skills, knowledge, and expertise necessary for the discharge of the responsibilities allocated to them. The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) further elaborates on these requirements through guidelines, emphasizing that individuals performing compliance, risk management, or internal audit roles must possess relevant professional experience and a deep understanding of the firm's business, risks, and regulatory obligations. For instance, the head of the compliance function is expected to have sufficient authority, resources, and access to all relevant information to fulfill their responsibilities effectively, implying a significant level of seniority and a robust background in financial regulation and operations.

In the United Kingdom, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) implements the Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), detailed within the FCA Handbook, particularly in SYSC (Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls). The SMCR aims to improve individual accountability in financial services by requiring firms to clearly allocate responsibilities to Senior Managers and to assess the fitness and propriety of individuals performing key functions. Senior Managers, who hold specific 'Senior Management Functions' (SMFs), must be approved by the FCA and meet rigorous 'fit and proper' criteria. This includes an assessment of their honesty, integrity, reputation, competence, capability, and financial soundness. For example, individuals holding SMF16 (Compliance Oversight) or SMF4 (Chief Risk Officer) are expected to demonstrate extensive experience in their respective fields, a thorough understanding of regulatory requirements, and the ability to effectively oversee complex compliance or risk frameworks. Furthermore, the Certification Regime requires firms to certify annually that individuals in 'Certification Functions' (roles that could cause significant harm to the firm or its customers) are fit and proper to perform their roles, based on similar criteria, thus extending the focus on qualifications beyond just senior leadership roles to a broader range of critical personnel.

The regulatory frameworks governing financial institutions across jurisdictions frequently impose stringent requirements concerning licensing, ownership, and control, particularly for entities engaged in sensitive activities such as the provision of credit information services. These frameworks aim to ensure financial stability, protect consumers, and prevent market abuse by scrutinizing the ultimate beneficial ownership and the influence exerted by significant shareholders.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and various prudential regulators, such as the Federal Reserve Board (FRB), implement rules that address these concerns. For instance, the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 (BHCA), as amended, establishes a comprehensive regulatory regime for bank holding companies and their subsidiaries. Section 2(a)(2) of the BHCA defines 'control' broadly, encompassing situations where an entity directly or indirectly owns, controls, or holds with power to vote 25 percent or more of any class of voting shares of a bank or company, controls the election of a majority of the directors or trustees of a bank or company, or exercises a controlling influence over the management or policies of a bank or company. These provisions are critical for determining the permissible 'Investment Ratio' and 'Equity Ownership' structures within the banking sector, particularly when assessing whether a financial institution or a related entity is subject to the Act's oversight. The distinction between 'Voting Rights' and the mere economic interest represented by 'Non-voting Shares' is paramount in such assessments, with the focus often placed on the ability to exert influence through voting power.

Furthermore, under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 13(d) mandates disclosure requirements for persons or groups who acquire beneficial ownership of more than 5 percent of a class of voting equity securities of a publicly traded company. This necessitates the filing of Schedule 13D or 13G, detailing the nature of the acquisition and any plans or proposals regarding the issuer. This mechanism provides transparency regarding significant 'Equity Ownership' and potential shifts in control that could impact a regulated entity, including those involved in the broader financial services industry, such as companies processing or disseminating credit information.

Across the Atlantic, the European Union's regulatory landscape, particularly under MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU on markets in financial instruments) and CRD IV (Directive 2013/36/EU on access to the activity of credit institutions and the prudential supervision of credit institutions and investment firms), similarly emphasizes robust ownership and control assessments.
